tier_reason: README Performance table gives Spaces' own absolute numbers plus rank against jemalloc, snmalloc, tcmalloc and Hoard on mimalloc-bench workloads; competitor numbers, CPU model and compiler version are absent, so first-party C despite public bench.sh.

corrections.compiler_and_flags: gcc -O3 -pthread -fPIC for spaces.c; bench.sh builds the mimalloc-bench workloads with $compiler -O3 -pthread against libspaces.a; how the competitor allocators were built is not stated
corrections.caveats: First-party table gives ranks and absolute numbers for Spaces only, not the competitors' numbers; the 'beats' lists differ per row (mleak beats only jemalloc and snmalloc; xmalloc-test beats snmalloc and tcmalloc; mstress beats tcmalloc and Hoard), and the allocator ranked #1 is never named (likely mimalloc). CPU model, core count, kernel and compiler version are not stated; repo has only 2 commits (2026-03-23 and 2026-03-29); x86-64 Linux only. Loses on glibc-thread (#6).

notes: Numbers match the README table exactly. MIT confirmed via LICENSE; 64 stars, not archived, last commit 2026-03-29.

tier_reason: Paper (arXiv 2508.20253; search results also list an IEEE Computer Architecture Letters 2025 version) reports gem5 full-system simulation speedups over jemalloc, TCMalloc and mimalloc, but every copy was egress-blocked, so the numbers are confirmed only through search snippets; kept at C pending a retier with paper access (peer-reviewed venue could justify B).

corrections.claimed_speedup: On 16-thread workloads: 1.75x over Jemalloc, 1.18x over TCMalloc, 1.15x over Mimalloc, 1.23x over Mallacc, 1.18x over Memento+; energy savings 1.69x/1.15x/1.12x over Jemalloc/TCMalloc/Mimalloc (search snippets). Per-thread-count Mimalloc figures (1.17x-1.25x at 1-16 threads) could not be confirmed.
corrections.workload: Multi-threaded allocation-heavy workloads in full-system gem5 simulation (AArch64) with McPAT power/area modelling; allocator runs on a lightweight microcontroller-grade support core (~1-2% chip area).
corrections.caveats: Hardware proposal evaluated only in gem5 simulation; not usable on existing CPUs and no code release found. arXiv, IEEE CAL author PDF (ut-sysml.ece.utexas.edu), themoonlight and pith.science all blocked here; numbers are snippet-only. The 1.75x/1.18x/1.15x figures are for 16-thread workloads, not an overall average.

notes: Search results name an IEEE CAL vol. 24 no. 2 (2025) version at ut-sysml.ece.utexas.edu/publications/prints/cal2025_li.pdf; a retier with paper access could move it to B. Authors: Ruihao Li, Lizy K. John et al. (UT Austin).

tier_reason: BENCHMARKS.md and BENCHMARKS_WASM.md show first-party plots (random-actions, heap efficiency, microbench, wasm-perf) with public bench code in benches/src and wasm-perf/, but no compiler, flags or CPU are stated and no numbers appear in text; C.

corrections.claimed_speedup: No numbers in text; BENCHMARKS_WASM.md concludes 'DLmalloc and RLSF's GlobalTlsf are worse in both size and performance to Talc' and 'If all you care about is performance, use Talc' (plots only).
corrections.caveats: Results are plots only, no compiler, flags or CPU stated. Author says jemalloc/mimalloc/system allocator are not compared and recommends them on hosted systems; notes the benchmark size/alignment distributions may be 'mildly fitted' to Talc and that Talc v4 was mediocre and RLSF 'walks all over' it (motivating v5). The win claimed is over DLmalloc, Rust's default wasm allocator. FRuSA is excluded from the heap-efficiency plot; the earlier claim that the author states Talc is slower than FRuSA under concurrency is not on the current pages.

notes: Real wasm/no_std allocator; recognizable incumbent is DLmalloc (Rust wasm default). MIT (LICENSE.md), 562 stars, last commit 2026-09-09, not archived or a fork.
